summary: Trump, Xi and Putin meet as a trio without a deal, Iran fires at Gulf bases again, Ukraine breaks a span of the Kerch Bridge, Israel's new majority moves on court laws, and Anthropic sets an IPO record.

question.text: Israel's new majority is voting to undo court laws the last government passed. If each new government can quickly reverse the last one's biggest changes, what happens over time to how people and businesses plan, and to how much they trust any single law?

read.title: What investors should know about Anthropic's unusual IPO
read.summary: A plain explainer of how this IPO differs from most: a public benefit company, a trust that can pick most of the board, and founders who keep a majority of votes, which shows that owning shares is not the same as controlling a company.

topics.heading: Trump, Xi and Putin hold first three-way talks in Shenzhen; no nuclear or Ukraine deal
topics.summary: The US, Chinese and Russian leaders met for about 90 minutes at APEC in Shenzhen, and no joint agreement on nuclear arms, Ukraine or Iran was announced.[^1][^5] Xi proposed crisis communication channels between the three, while China says Trump and Xi agreed to draft an action plan for steadier US-China ties.[^1][^3]

lead.title: The Latest: Trump meets with Putin and Xi in China

alsoReported.title: Trump, Xi, Putin begin historic meeting with Ukraine war on agenda
Putin, Trump, Xi conclude trilateral meeting after about 90 minutes

article: On Thursday, Donald Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin held the first ever three-way meeting of US, Chinese and Russian leaders, on the sidelines of the APEC summit in Shenzhen. Russia's TASS news agency said it lasted about 90 minutes.[^5] AP reported no specific agreements on nuclear arms, Ukraine or Iran.[^1]

Trump opened by saying "We are really making history" and that the three countries are "uniquely positioned" to discuss cutting the number of nuclear weapons, while admitting that giving them up is "not an easy thing to do".[^1][^2] China has repeatedly refused to join arms talks with the US and Russia, whose arsenals are far larger.[^2] According to Chinese state TV, Xi proposed that the three set up crisis communication and prevention channels to reduce misjudgments, and argued against "decoupling", meaning cutting economic ties.[^1]

Before that, Trump and Xi met one to one, their third meeting this year. China's Xinhua agency called the talks "positive and constructive" and said both sides agreed to draft an action plan for a stable relationship. Xi also told Trump the US should do "the right thing" on Taiwan.[^3] Trump said he and Xi both feel strongly that oil must keep flowing through the Strait of Hormuz.[^2]

Trump also met Putin for about 40 minutes, their first in-person meeting in over a year. Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov said the war in Ukraine dominated.[^4] Trump told Xi he wanted help ending that war: "I'd like to see it ended."[^4] Putin spoke of "numerous shared interests" in settling regional conflicts, including Ukraine, and criticised Western sanctions.[^2]

Why it matters: these three countries hold most of the world's nuclear weapons. Ukraine and European leaders were not in the room, which adds to European worries about deals made over their heads.[^4] My read: the day produced words and a possible process, not commitments. The crisis-channel idea and the US-China action plan are the pieces to watch; China's stance on nuclear talks did not visibly move.[^1][^2][^3]
topics.differences: Trump says the three powers are well placed to reduce nuclear arsenals; China has repeatedly objected to joining such talks, and Xi focused on crisis communication, trade and Taiwan.[^1][^2][^3] The Kremlin says Ukraine was the main topic of the Trump-Putin meeting; Putin used the summit to criticise Western sanctions.[^2][^4]

topics.heading: Iran fires at US bases in Kuwait and Bahrain and says three tankers hit mines near Hormuz
topics.summary: A day after the US struck Qeshm Island, Iran targeted a US air base in Kuwait and sites in Bahrain; both countries say they intercepted the attacks without damage.[^6] Iran's navy says three tankers hit mines east of the Strait of Hormuz, as Tehran and Oman discuss a shipping corridor.[^7][^8]

lead.title: Iran widens Gulf attacks by targeting U.S. air base in Kuwait, sites in Bahrain

alsoReported.title: Iran says 3 tankers caught fire after hitting mines east of Hormuz Strait
Iran, Oman move closer to Hormuz shipping 'deal': What it means for global oil trade

article: Early on Wednesday, Iran fired at Ali Al Salem, a US air base in Kuwait, and launched several attacks on Bahrain, home of the US Navy's 5th Fleet, AP reports. It was the first wave of this kind in about two months.[^6] Kuwait's military said it intercepted drones with no immediate damage, and Bahrain reported no damage or casualties. Kuwait's foreign ministry called the attacks "criminal".[^6]

The attacks followed Tuesday's US strike on a Revolutionary Guard missile site on Qeshm Island. Iran says its strikes on Bahrain answer US drone surveillance and an attack on Iranian communications towers.[^6]

At sea, Iran's navy said on Thursday that three oil tankers caught fire and stopped after hitting naval mines east of the strait. It said the ships had switched off their tracking systems and entered a "forbidden" area, and that all ships must use corridors "authorized" by Iran's forces.[^7] These are Iran's claims; the ships were not named.[^7]

On the diplomatic side, Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi met Oman's Sultan Haitham bin Tarik in Muscat on Wednesday. Iranian officials say they have a "mutual understanding" with Oman on a shipping corridor through the strait, which the two countries border, but no final deal was announced and it still needs formal approval.[^8] Wider talks have stalled despite mediation by Qatar, AP reports.[^6] In Shenzhen, Trump said he and Xi both want oil to keep flowing through Hormuz.[^2]

Why it matters: a US naval blockade is squeezing Iran's economy, and an analyst at Israel's INSS think tank calls Iran's moves "deliberate, calibrated escalation" to raise the blockade's cost. An International Crisis Group analyst warns that the build-up of incidents raises the risk of miscalculation.[^6] My read: the Iran-Oman corridor is the one track that could lower the danger to shipping; without it, expect more tit-for-tat.
topics.differences: Iran says its strikes respond to US drone flights and attacks; the US called its Qeshm strike a response to an Iranian attack on a US radar in Bahrain.[^6] Iran's navy says the mined tankers were in a "forbidden" zone with tracking switched off; there is no independent account of the tanker incidents yet.[^7]

topics.heading: Ukraine knocks out a road span of the Kerch Bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea
topics.summary: Ukraine hit the bridge with drones and missiles, and its military says a road arch and span collapsed while the rail line stayed up but was damaged.[^9] The Kremlin says the bridge will be restored; a Ukrainian expert says that could take a year or more.[^9][^11]

lead.title: 'The symbol of the occupation': Ukraine destroys span of Kerch Bridge linking Russia with Crimea

alsoReported.title: 'Crimea is turning into an island': How Ukraine hit Putin's prized bridge
Russia says the Crimean bridge will come back 'even better.' That may take a while

article: Overnight into Tuesday, Ukraine struck the Kerch Bridge, also called the Crimean Bridge, with drones and missiles. It is the only direct road and rail link between Russia and Crimea, which Russia annexed in 2014.[^9] Ukraine's General Staff said an arch and a span of the road section collapsed, cutting road traffic, while the railway stayed standing with one arch damaged. AP could not verify videos Ukraine released.[^9]

President Volodymyr Zelenskyy called it an "unprecedented" operation, the last stage of a weeks-long campaign that first wore down Russian air defences. He said Ukrainian-made drones, Neptune missiles and Flamingo cruise missiles were used.[^9][^10] Russia's Investigative Committee said only that the bridge was damaged. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said it would be restored, and Crimea's Russian-installed governor said rail traffic resumed on Tuesday afternoon.[^9] Russian media called the damage "insignificant".[^10]
The same day, Russian ballistic missiles hit two of Kyiv's bridges over the Dnipro River, killing at least two people, and Russian strikes on Zaporizhzhia killed two more, AP reports.[^9]

Why it matters: the 19-kilometre bridge, opened in 2018, is a symbol of Russia's hold on Crimea, and Kyiv considers it illegal.[^10] A Ukrainian aviation expert estimates restoring the span could take "a year or even longer".[^11] Al Jazeera notes the fallen arch lies in the deepest part of the strait and could block freighters carrying grain, though a Bremen University researcher argues the strike matters little militarily because the bridge has carried almost no military traffic for a year.[^10]

My read: the strike came just before Putin left for Shenzhen, and it strengthens Ukraine's hand symbolically more than on the battlefield. No date has been set for the next US-mediated round of peace talks.[^9][^10]
topics.differences: Ukraine says the road section is out of action; Russian officials acknowledged damage without detail, and Russian media called it "insignificant".[^9][^10] AP describes the bridge as a route for both military and civilian supplies; the Kremlin accuses Kyiv of striking civilian targets, while a Bremen University researcher says it has carried almost no military traffic for a year.[^9][^10]

topics.heading: Israel's new Knesset majority takes a first vote to repeal Netanyahu's court laws
topics.summary: A day after electing its own speaker, the Eisenkot-led bloc passed early votes to repeal three laws from Netanyahu's judicial overhaul.[^45][^47] The same day, Naftali Bennett met Netanyahu privately, which some in his own bloc called a "strategic disaster".[^48]

lead.title: Israel's Knesset advances bills repealing Netanyahu's judicial overhaul laws

alsoReported.title: Eisenkot bloc begins push to reverse Netanyahu's laws with judicial overhaul repeal
'Strategic disaster': Bennett-Netanyahu meeting sparks backlash within Eisenkot bloc amid unity talks

article: On Wednesday, Israel's parliament, the Knesset, voted in a "preliminary reading", the first of four votes a bill needs, to repeal three laws passed by Benjamin Netanyahu's outgoing government.[^45] One gave politicians more say in choosing judges, one would let ministers ignore the attorney general's legal advice, and one changed how broadcasters are regulated.[^45][^47] Each passed with between 63 and 67 votes against about 47 to 49.[^45][^46]

The votes came a day after the bloc led by Gadi Eisenkot, with Arab-led parties' support, elected Matan Kahana as speaker.[^45] A committee waived the usual waiting period; the Knesset's legal adviser said that is allowed when there are strong grounds for urgency.[^46] The bills now go back to committee.[^45][^47]

Justice Minister Yariv Levin, who designed the overhaul, called the repeal "corruption" and warned that "everything you are trying to repeal will return".[^45][^47] Democrats lawmaker Efrat Rayten said the changes are meant "not to destroy, but to repair."[^45]

Meanwhile, Naftali Bennett, a leader in Eisenkot's bloc, met Netanyahu for about two and a half hours without telling Eisenkot first.[^48] Bennett's allies say he would back a unity government only if Eisenkot serves first as prime minister.[^49] After a bloc meeting, its leaders said replacing Netanyahu is a "top priority".[^49]

Why it matters: no government has formed since the October 27 election, and Netanyahu leads a caretaker government.[^45] My read: the votes show the bloc can pass laws, but the Bennett meeting shows its unity is not guaranteed.
topics.differences: Outlets give slightly different tallies: the Jerusalem Post reports 67-47 on judicial selection and 63-47 on the attorney general law, while Ynet reports 63-47 on judicial selection.[^45][^46] Eisenkot's bloc says Likud demanded Netanyahu stay prime minister with no state inquiry into October 7; a Likud source disputed parts of that.[^48]

topics.heading: Anthropic prices the biggest IPO on record at $83 a share; Nasdaq trading starts today
topics.summary: Anthropic sold shares at $83 each on Wednesday, above its planned range, raising about $81 billion and valuing the AI company at about $1.5 trillion.[^40][^41] Its stock is due to start trading on the Nasdaq on Thursday under the ticker ANT.[^40]

lead.title: Anthropic prices its IPO at $83 per share, valuing the AI giant at $1.5 trillion

alsoReported.title: Anthropic prices blockbuster IPO at $83 a share, source says

article: An IPO, or initial public offering, is when a private company first sells shares to the public. On Wednesday Anthropic set its price at $83 a share, above the $70 to $78 range it had planned, AP reports.[^40] It also sold more shares than first planned, about 980 million, and raised about $81 billion. That beats SpaceX's roughly $75 billion in June as the largest IPO on record.[^40][^41] Trading is due to begin on the Nasdaq some time after the market opens at 9:30 a.m. on Thursday.[^40]

Reuters says the price gives Anthropic a value of about $1.5 trillion, counting all shares that could exist in future, and about $1.1 trillion counting only current shares.[^41] Its filings show third-quarter revenue of $16.96 billion and an operating loss of $567 million.[^41] The company has also signed deals to spend nearly $900 billion on computing in coming years, $70 billion of it in the next 12 months, and has $6.2 billion in debt.[^40]

Anthropic is a "public benefit corporation", which means it must weigh the public good alongside profits, and a long-term benefit trust can elect or remove most of its board.[^40] A note on bias: Anthropic makes Claude, the AI that writes this brief.

Why it matters: investors are treating the sale as a test of whether the AI boom is a bubble. Analyst Dan Ives saw "strong appetite" for the shares.[^40] AP points to risks, including possible new rules from a Democratic-led Congress next year, local opposition to data centres, and several tech companies that recently dropped plans to go public.[^40] One fund manager told Reuters that "one listing won't settle the debate."[^41]
My read: first-day price moves are mostly noise. The steadier signals are the next few quarterly reports, and whether the money raised keeps up with the computing bills.
topics.differences: Some investors, like Baillie Gifford, argue most of AI's value will go to companies "at the frontier"; Anthropic's own filing warns that computing capacity it has contracted "may be delayed, repriced, reduced, or not delivered."[^41]

topics.heading: Fossil teeth suggest Homo erectus lived in southern China far later than thought
topics.summary: Two studies in Nature identify eight teeth from caves in southern China as Homo erectus, dated to between about 324,000 and 184,000 years ago.[^42][^43] Chemical clues suggest these early humans lived in rainforest, a habitat once linked only to our own species.[^42][^43]

lead.title: Archaic human species Homo erectus mastered the rainforest in China

alsoReported.title: Homo Erectus May Have Survived in China 200,000 Years Longer Than We Thought
Homo erectus Thrived in Chinese Rainforest Far Later than Thought

article: Homo erectus was an early human species that appeared in Africa about two million years ago. It was the first known human species to leave Africa and is thought to have been the first to use fire.[^42] Scientists had believed it disappeared from mainland Asia around 400,000 years ago.[^42][^43]

On Wednesday, two research teams published studies in the journal Nature on nine teeth from the Baxian and Naxian caves in Guangxi, southern China.[^44] Based on tooth shape and, in some cases, ancient proteins preserved in the enamel, they say eight belong to Homo erectus.[^42][^43] The teeth were dated to between about 324,000 and 184,000 years ago, which would mean the species survived there roughly 200,000 years longer than many researchers assumed.[^43]

Chemical signals in the teeth, called isotopes, record what an animal ate and drank. They suggest this group lived in rainforest, alongside orangutans and an extinct forest elephant.[^43] Other chemical traces suggest they travelled widely, possibly towards what is now northern Vietnam.[^42] Lead researcher Kira Westaway called the group "flexible, adaptable and mobile".[^42] The ninth tooth is a puzzle: co-author Frido Welker said it "could be Denisovan, but also something unknown."[^42]

Why it matters: rainforests were seen as a frontier that only modern humans could cross, said Marwick, a University of Washington archaeologist not involved in the work.[^43] Potts, a Smithsonian scientist also not involved, said "the identification looks really solid."[^43] The research team says the dates suggest these populations probably never met Homo sapiens.[^42]
My read: this is careful work, but it rests on a handful of teeth. Expect more digging and dating in the region before the picture is settled.
